A pipeline runner called mipula-27 is to receive plugins from the plugin registry.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
* To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
* Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
* The proposed set installs cleanly when every pinned version is listed in the plugin registry, every requirement of every pinned version names a plugin that is pinned at a version meeting all of its bounds, the runtime of the target environment meets every runtime bound of every pinned version, and no conflict entry of a pinned version applies to another pin.
* Entries of versions that are not pinned are irrelevant.
* No plugin is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a plugin that has no pin, that requirement fails.
* Pinning a plugin that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.
* Runtime bounds are checked against the runtime of the target environment; a version marked 'any' runs on every runtime.
* If a pinned version has a 'conflicts with' entry naming another plugin and that plugin is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about plugins that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

Proposed install on ostrvar-24, a game server: the extensions pinned at the end, taken from the extension catalogue below.

Rules of this check:
* To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
* After an extension name come one or more bounds separated by commas, and every bound must hold: >=V at least V, >V newer than V, <=V at most V, <V older than V, ==V exactly V, !=V any version except V.
* The set is clean only if the extension catalogue lists every pinned version, every requirement of a pinned version is met by the pin of the required extension, each runtime bound of a pinned version holds for the environment's runtime, and none of the pinned versions has a conflict entry that applies to another pin.
* Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the extension catalogue says about other versions plays no part.
* Only pinned extensions get installed; a required extension that has no pin counts as unmet.
* A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
* Runtime bounds are checked against the runtime of the target environment; a version marked 'any' runs on every runtime.
* If a pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry naming another extension and that extension is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about extensions that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

What the list shows:
- ticket: identifier of the visitor
- class: the service class (1 = most urgent)
- entered: time the visitor entered (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the visitor; "-" means no marker
- booked: time of the booked appointment, "-" if there is none
- desk: expected desk time in minutes

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. The flag "carer" moves a visitor up one class.
2. A visitor with a lower class number goes before a visitor with a higher class number.
3. Among visitors of one class, a visitor with a due booked time is ahead of a visitor without a due one.
4. Last tie-break: the visitor with the lower ticket number goes first.

How to read the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between visitors that all rules before it leave level.
- Rule 1 does not order anything by itself: it sets the class that the later rules use.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Any task carrying the flag "rush" is lifted by one class.
2. The tasks are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
3. Among tasks of one class, a task with a due reserved start is ahead of a task without a due one.
4. If tasks are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Conventions:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- Rule 1 changes the class of a task and is applied to every task before anything is compared; in the rules after it, "class" means the class after this change.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- Class 1 is the top: a task never moves above class 1.
- A task that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- A reserved start counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the reserved start was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting tasks, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.

Rules of this check:
1. Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
2. Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
3. A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the package index lists; for each pinned version, each package it requires is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry that applies to another pin.

5. No package is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a package that has no pin, that requirement fails.
6. Extra pins are fine: a pinned package that nothing requires is harmless as long as its own entry is satisfied.
7. The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
8. Conflicts ('cannot be combined with'): a pinned version that names a package P with a bound blocks the set exactly when P is pinned at a version meeting that bound; if P has no pin, or its pin misses the bound, nothing happens.

Export request handling

Rules:
Rule 1. When the export size does not exceed 100 records: Approve the request.
Rule 2. When the data region is either Zanbel or Zerbel and the account age is 270 days or less and the personal data flag is yes: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 3. When the account age is 30 days or less and the record shows no for the consent on file flag: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 4. When the data region is anything other than Mardex and the number of exports in the last 30 days is not below 2: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 5. When the number of exports in the last 30 days is 1 or less: Approve the request.
Rule 6. When the case has the consent on file flag set to yes: Approve the request.
Rule 7. When the number of exports in the last 30 days is more than 3: Deny the request.
Rule 8. When the personal data flag is set to no: Approve the request.
Rule 9. When the record shows yes for the personal data flag and the account age is not more than 30 days and the number of exports in the last 30 days is 3 or more: Deny the request.
Rule 10. When the export size is not below 5000 records: Deny the request.
Rule 11. When the personal data flag is yes and the account age lies in the range 14 to 270 days inclusive: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 12. When the record shows yes for the personal data flag and the data region on record is Melkar and the export size is 50000 records or higher: Deny the request.

Exceptions:
- If the export size is above 1000 records, Rule 6 does not apply.
- If the account age is less than 30 days and the record shows no for the consent on file flag, Rule 5 does not apply.
- If the account age is under 30 days, Rule 1 does not apply.
- If the number of exports in the last 30 days does not exceed 1 and the export size does not exceed 5000 records, Rule 3 does not apply.

Conflicts and default:
- In a conflict between rules, the later rule in the list prevails.
- A request that no rule covers is denied.

q.instructions: Does the proposed set install cleanly in the target environment?

state:
sarndru-20 (a field controller) should get the modules listed under the pins, drawn from the module feed.

Rules of this check:
1. Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
2. Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
3. A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the module feed lists; for each pinned version, each module it needs is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'conflicts with' entry that applies to another pin.
4. Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the module feed says about other versions plays no part.
5. Nothing is installed besides the pins, so a requirement on a module without a pin is not met.
6. A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
7. A runtime bound of a pinned version is met when the runtime of the target environment satisfies it; 'any' sets no runtime bound.
8. An entry 'conflicts with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about a module without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

state:
A game server called ostrvek-14 is to receive extensions from the extension catalogue.

Conventions:
* Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. Runtime versions (two parts) follow the same order, so 4.11 is later than 4.9.
* Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
* A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the extension catalogue lists; for each pinned version, each extension it depends on is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry that applies to another pin.
* Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the extension catalogue says about other versions plays no part.
* Nothing is installed besides the pins, so a requirement on an extension without a pin is not met.
* A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
* Runtime bounds are checked against the runtime of the target environment; a version marked 'any' runs on every runtime.
* If a pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry naming another extension and that extension is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about extensions that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

What the list shows:
- ticket: identifier of the visitor
- class: the service class (1 = most urgent)
- entered: time the visitor entered (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the visitor; "-" means no marker
- booked: time of the booked appointment, "-" if there is none
- desk: expected desk time in minutes

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. The flag "carer" moves a visitor up one class.
2. A visitor with a lower class number goes before a visitor with a higher class number.
3. Among visitors of one class, a visitor with a due booked time is ahead of a visitor without a due one.
4. Last tie-break: the visitor with the lower ticket number goes first.

How to read the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between visitors that all rules before it leave level.
- Rule 1 does not order anything by itself: it sets the class that the later rules use.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- After a class change a visitor is treated like every other visitor of its new class.
- A booked time is due when its time is the current time or earlier; a later one is not due yet.
- Two visitors that are both due, or both not due (no booked time, or one that is still to come), stay level under this rule.
- Rank every waiting visitor once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Every visitor has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
- Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. Runtime versions (two parts) follow the same order, so 4.11 is later than 4.9.
- Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
- The set is clean only if the module feed lists every pinned version, every requirement of a pinned version is met by the pin of the required module, each runtime bound of a pinned version holds for the environment's runtime, and none of the pinned versions has a conflict entry that applies to another pin.
- Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the module feed says about other versions plays no part.
- No module is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a module that has no pin, that requirement fails.
- A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
- A runtime bound of a pinned version is met when the runtime of the target environment satisfies it; 'any' sets no runtime bound.
- An entry 'cannot be combined with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about a module without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

q.instructions: Does the proposed set install cleanly in the target environment?

state:
A field controller called ostrkam-16 is to receive modules from the module feed.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
1. Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. Runtime versions (two parts) follow the same order, so 4.11 is later than 4.9.
2. After a module name come one or more bounds separated by commas, and every bound must hold: >=V at least V, >V newer than V, <=V at most V, <V older than V, ==V exactly V, !=V any version except V.
3. The set is clean only if the module feed lists every pinned version, every requirement of a pinned version is met by the pin of the required module, each runtime bound of a pinned version holds for the environment's runtime, and none of the pinned versions has a conflict entry that applies to another pin.
4. Entries of versions that are not pinned are irrelevant.
5. Only pinned modules get installed; a required module that has no pin counts as unmet.
6. Pinning a module that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.

What the list shows:

- flag: at most one marker per vessel ("-" = none)
- window: start of the booked berth window ("-" = none)

Ordering rules (apply them in this order):
1. A vessel that has waited at least 25 minutes moves up one class.
2. Lower class number first.
3. Within the same class, vessels whose berth window is due go first.
4. If vessels are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Notes on the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- First apply rule 1 to each vessel; from rule 2 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- No vessel can go higher than class 1; a vessel of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- After a class change a vessel is treated like every other vessel of its new class.
- The waiting time of a vessel is counted in minutes from the time under "anchored" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- A wait of exactly 25 minutes counts as at least 25 minutes.
- Due means that the time under "window" has been reached: it is equal to the current time or before it.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the berth window was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- Rank every waiting vessel once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- Every vessel has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

How access is decided:
1. A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
2. Assignments reach downward only: the section where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; sections beside it or above it are not.
3. A sealed section blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher section covers neither the sealed section nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed section itself, or at a section below it, is not affected by that seal, and sections outside the sealed section are not affected either.
4. A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
5. The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
6. Deny entries win over assignments. An entry blocks its action for the user it names, or for every member of the group it names (members through nested groups included), on its section and on everything below that section, sealed or not. It blocks that single action only; requests for other actions are judged as if the entry were not there, also when the actions are linked by an inclusion.

3. A sealed folder blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher folder covers neither the sealed folder nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed folder itself, or at a folder below it, is not affected by that seal, and folders outside the sealed folder are not affected either.
4. A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
5. Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
6. Decision: a request is allowed when some assignment that counts for the requester covers the requested folder with a role that allows the requested action. In every other case it is not allowed.

q.instructions: Does the proposed set install cleanly in the target environment?

state:
vobath-06 (a game server) should get the extensions listed under the pins, drawn from the extension catalogue.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
1. Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
2. Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
3. A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the extension catalogue lists; for each pinned version, each extension it needs is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'conflicts with' entry that applies to another pin.
4. Entries of versions that are not pinned are irrelevant.
5. No extension is added automatically: if a pinned version requires an extension that has no pin, that requirement fails.
6. Pinning an extension that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.
7. The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
8. An entry 'conflicts with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about an extension without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

state:
Proposed install on peskgan-28, a robot controller: the components pinned at the end, taken from the component depot below.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
* To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. Runtime versions (two parts) follow the same order, so 4.11 is later than 4.9.
* Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
* The proposed set installs cleanly when every pinned version is listed in the component depot, every requirement of every pinned version names a component that is pinned at a version meeting all of its bounds, the runtime of the target environment meets every runtime bound of every pinned version, and no conflict entry of a pinned version applies to another pin.
* Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the component depot says about other versions plays no part.
* No component is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a component that has no pin, that requirement fails.
* Extra pins are fine: a pinned component that nothing requires is harmless as long as its own entry is satisfied.
* The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
* If a pinned version has a 'clashes with' entry naming another component and that component is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about components that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

Rules of this check:
* Versions are compared number by number from the left, each number as a whole number: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.3, and 2.0.0 is newer than 1.12.7. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.

state:
An analysis workstation called skelilo-34 is to receive packages from the package index.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
1. Versions are compared number by number from the left, each number as a whole number: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.3, and 2.0.0 is newer than 1.12.7. Runtime versions have two numbers and are compared the same way (3.10 is newer than 3.9).
2. Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
3. A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the package index lists; for each pinned version, each package it requires is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry that applies to another pin.
4. Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the package index says about other versions plays no part.
5. Nothing is installed besides the pins, so a requirement on a package without a pin is not met.
6. A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
7. Runtime bounds are checked against the runtime of the target environment; a version marked 'any' runs on every runtime.
8. If a pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry naming another package and that package is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about packages that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

What follows are the access rules and the current permission records of an invented building access system.

Access rules (they apply exactly as written):
1. An assignment gives one role to one user or to one group. An assignment to a group counts for every member of the group. Membership passes through nested groups: when group X is listed as a member of group Y, all members of X (also those X has through its own nested groups) are members of Y. It does not pass the other way: a user listed directly in Y is not thereby a member of X.
2. An assignment is made at one zone. It covers that zone and every zone below it (directly or further down), and nothing else.
3. A sealed zone blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher zone covers neither the sealed zone nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed zone itself, or at a zone below it, is not affected by that seal, and zones outside the sealed zone are not affected either.
4. A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
5. The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
6. Deny entries win over assignments. An entry blocks its action for the user it names, or for every member of the group it names (members through nested groups included), on its zone and on everything below that zone, sealed or not. It blocks that single action only; requests for other actions are judged as if the entry were not there, also when the actions are linked by an inclusion.
7. A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested zone and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.

Meaning of the fields:
- ticket: queue identifier of the task
- class: queue class, class 1 being the most urgent
- submitted: time the task was submitted (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the task; "-" means no marker
- reserved: time of the reserved start, "-" if there is none
- runtime: expected run time in minutes, whole minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Once the waiting time of a task is at least 50 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. Lower class number first.
3. Within the same class, tasks whose reserved start is due go first.
4. Lower ticket number first.

Notes on the rules:
- Read the rules from top to bottom; a later rule is used only to separate tasks that every earlier rule leaves level.
- Rule 1 does not order anything by itself: it sets the class that the later rules use.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- No task can go higher than class 1; a task of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- A task that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "submitted" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- "At least 50 minutes" includes exactly 50 minutes; 49 minutes are not enough.
- Due means that the time under "reserved" has been reached: it is equal to the current time or before it.
- Two tasks that are both due, or both not due (no reserved start, or one that is still to come), stay level under this rule.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two tasks have the same one.

Asked: the task that is first in the order

Location: Ibettra print room, production queue 6
Clock at the moment of the decision: 12:53

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Any task carrying the flag "rush" is lifted by one class.
2. The tasks are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
3. Among tasks of one class, a task with a due reserved start is ahead of a task without a due one.
4. If tasks are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Conventions:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- Rule 1 changes the class of a task and is applied to every task before anything is compared; in the rules after it, "class" means the class after this change.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- Class 1 is the top: a task never moves above class 1.
- A task that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- A reserved start counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the reserved start was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting tasks, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- Ticket numbers are the digits after the dash, compared as numbers, and they are unique.

Rules for data export requests

A game server called ostreth-44 is to receive extensions from the extension catalogue.

Rules of this check:
* Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. Runtime versions (two parts) follow the same order, so 4.11 is later than 4.9.
* After an extension name come one or more bounds separated by commas, and every bound must hold: >=V at least V, >V newer than V, <=V at most V, <V older than V, ==V exactly V, !=V any version except V.
* A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the extension catalogue lists; for each pinned version, each extension it requires is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'conflicts with' entry that applies to another pin.
* Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the extension catalogue says about other versions plays no part.
* Only pinned extensions get installed; a required extension that has no pin counts as unmet.
* Pinning an extension that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.
* A runtime bound of a pinned version is met when the runtime of the target environment satisfies it; 'any' sets no runtime bound.
* If a pinned version has a 'conflicts with' entry naming another extension and that extension is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about extensions that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

Data export policy

(11) The request must be denied if the export size is more than 50000 records and the number of exports in the last 30 days is 3 or more.
(12) The request must be denied if the legal hold flag is yes and the account age is 180 days or less.

EXCEPTIONS

Exception to Rule 4: it is not applied when the account age exceeds 90 days and the data region on record is Melpen.

GENERAL
If two applicable rules lead to different outcomes, the lower-numbered rule decides.

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 60 minutes lifts a vessel by one class.
2. A vessel with the flag "tidal" counts one class more urgent.
3. A vessel with a lower class number goes before a vessel with a higher class number.
4. Of two vessels, the one with the earlier time under "anchored" is ahead.
5. Last tie-break: the vessel with the lower ticket number goes first.

Notes on the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each vessel; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- Class 1 is the top: a vessel never moves above class 1.
- A vessel that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- The waiting time of a vessel is counted in minutes from the time under "anchored" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- A wait of exactly 60 minutes counts as at least 60 minutes.
- Rules 1 and 2 add up: a vessel that meets both moves up two classes (but never above class 1).
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting vessels, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two vessels have the same one.

- A reserved start counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.

- The order is worked out once, for all waiting tasks, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.

Rule 10. Approve the request when the case has the contractor status flag set to no and the case has the open incident flag set to no and the case has the on-call duty flag set to yes.
Rule 11. Deny the request when the requested access period is more than 30 days.
Rule 12. Escalate the request to a human reviewer when the tenure is within 30 to 180 days with both limits included.

- If the manager approval flag is yes, Rule 4 does not apply.
- If the on-call duty flag is set to yes, Rule 11 does not apply.

Conflicts and default:
- When rules conflict, the rule with the lower number wins.
- When none of the rules applies, deny the request.

state.policy:
Refund handling rules

General provisions
- In a conflict between rules, the later rule in the list prevails.
- If no rule applies, the request is denied.

Rules
1. Approve the request when the record shows yes for the proof of purchase flag and the account age is above 365 days and the plan tier equals T3.
2. Escalate the request to a human reviewer when the refund amount is more than 250 EUR and the plan tier is either T3 or T4.
3. Deny the request when the refund amount exceeds 400 EUR and the region differs from Velvane.
4. Approve the request when the proof of purchase flag is yes and the refund amount is under 150 EUR.
5. Deny the request when the case has the fraud alert flag set to yes and the record shows no for the proof of purchase flag.
6. Deny the request when the number of earlier refunds is not below 2.
7. Approve the request when the refund amount is under 200 EUR and the fraud alert flag is set to no.
8. Escalate the request to a human reviewer when the proof of purchase flag is set to no and the number of earlier refunds is not below 4.

Exceptions
- If the record shows no for the fraud alert flag and the account age is at least 540 days, Rule 2 does not apply.
- If the account age is below 120 days, Rule 4 does not apply.
- If the account age is not below 90 days, Rule 3 does not apply.

Rules of this check:
* Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
* After a component name come one or more bounds separated by commas, and every bound must hold: >=V at least V, >V newer than V, <=V at most V, <V older than V, ==V exactly V, !=V any version except V.
* A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the component depot lists; for each pinned version, each component it needs is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'clashes with' entry that applies to another pin.
* Requirements and other entries of versions without a pin do not matter.
* No component is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a component that has no pin, that requirement fails.
* Pinning a component that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.
* The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
* An entry 'clashes with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about a component without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

A field controller called mipilo-12 is to receive modules from the module feed.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
- To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. Runtime versions have two numbers and are compared the same way (3.10 is newer than 3.9).
- Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
- A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the module feed lists; for each pinned version, each module it needs is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry that applies to another pin.
- Requirements and other entries of versions without a pin do not matter.
- Nothing is installed besides the pins, so a requirement on a module without a pin is not met.
- A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
- Runtime bounds are checked against the runtime of the target environment; a version marked 'any' runs on every runtime.
- If a pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry naming another module and that module is pinned at a version inside the given bound, the set is not clean (whichever side lists it); entries about modules that are not pinned, or whose pin lies outside the bound, are harmless.

- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- Once moved, a job competes inside its new class on equal terms with the jobs already there.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting jobs, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.

Rules of this check:

- Entries of versions that are not pinned are irrelevant.
- No plugin is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a plugin that has no pin, that requirement fails.
- Extra pins are fine: a pinned plugin that nothing requires is harmless as long as its own entry is satisfied.
- The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
- Conflicts ('cannot be combined with'): a pinned version that names a plugin P with a bound blocks the set exactly when P is pinned at a version meeting that bound; if P has no pin, or its pin misses the bound, nothing happens.

Rules of this check:

state:
Access export of an invented document workspace. The rules in this export decide every request.

How access is decided:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- Assignments reach downward only: the folder where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; folders beside it or above it are not.
- Sealing cuts off what comes from above. If the requested folder is a sealed folder or lies below one, an assignment made above that sealed folder does not cover it. Assignments made at the sealed folder or below it work as usual, and a sealed folder elsewhere in the tree has no effect.
- A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
- Where the inclusion list states that one action includes another, permission for the first counts as permission for the second, and likewise onward along several such lines. There are no unlisted inclusions, and the included action never brings the including one.
- A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested folder and that role allows the requested action.

state:
Service point: Ashorrin terminal, berth allocation post 9

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 60 minutes lifts a vessel by one class.
2. A vessel with the flag "tidal" counts one class more urgent.
3. A vessel with a lower class number goes before a vessel with a higher class number.
4. Of two vessels, the one with the earlier time under "anchored" is ahead.
5. Last tie-break: the vessel with the lower ticket number goes first.

Notes on the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each vessel; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- Class 1 is the top: a vessel never moves above class 1.
- A vessel that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- The waiting time of a vessel is counted in minutes from the time under "anchored" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- A wait of exactly 60 minutes counts as at least 60 minutes.
- Rules 1 and 2 add up: a vessel that meets both moves up two classes (but never above class 1).
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting vessels, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two vessels have the same one.

Rules of this check:
- To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. Runtime versions have two numbers and are compared the same way (3.10 is newer than 3.9).

- No plugin is added automatically: if a pinned version requires a plugin that has no pin, that requirement fails.

- The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).

state:
Access export of an invented document workspace. The rules in this export decide every request.

How access is decided:
1. A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
2. The role of an assignment is valid on the folder named in the assignment and on all folders below that folder at any depth, not on any other folder.
3. Sealing cuts off what comes from above. If the requested folder is a sealed folder or lies below one, an assignment made above that sealed folder does not cover it. Assignments made at the sealed folder or below it work as usual, and a sealed folder elsewhere in the tree has no effect.
4. The actions a role allows are its own actions plus the actions of the role it extends, plus those of the role that one extends, and so on. Nothing is passed in the opposite direction, from the extending role to the extended one.
5. Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
6. A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one folder. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested folder is the named folder or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.
7. A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested folder and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.

state.policy:
Export request handling

RULES
1. A request for which the consent on file flag is set to yes and the number of exports in the last 30 days is under 2 and the record shows no for the personal data flag is approved.
2. A request for which the account age does not exceed 120 days and the case has the legal hold flag set to yes is escalated to a human reviewer.
3. A request for which the export size is above 25000 records and the legal hold flag is set to yes is denied.
4. A request for which the consent on file flag is set to no and the case has the personal data flag set to yes and the plan tier is not T1 is denied.
5. A request for which the export size is less than 500 records and the record shows no for the legal hold flag is approved.
6. A request for which the plan tier is any of T3, T2 or T1 and the export size exceeds 100000 records and the number of exports in the last 30 days is 3 or higher is denied.
7. A request for which the record shows no for the verified requester flag is escalated to a human reviewer.
8. A request for which the record shows yes for the verified requester flag and the case has the consent on file flag set to yes is approved.

EXCEPTIONS
Exception to Rule 3: it is not applied when the account age is at least 180 days and the consent on file flag is yes.
Exception to Rule 1: it is not applied when the export size is greater than 25000 records.
Exception to Rule 8: it is not applied when the account age is not more than 270 days.

GENERAL
When rules conflict, the rule with the higher number wins.
By default a request is escalated to a human reviewer unless a rule says otherwise.

What follows are the access rules and the current permission records of an invented building access system.

Request: user p.laltez asks to inspect at the zone corridor.

How access is decided:
- Each assignment names a role and either a user or a group; if it names a group, every member of the group holds the role. Groups may list other groups as members. A user belongs to a group if the group lists the user or lists a group the user belongs to, over any number of steps. Belonging never runs downward: the users listed in an outer group do not belong to the groups listed inside it.
- The role of an assignment is valid on the zone named in the assignment and on all zones below that zone at any depth, not on any other zone.
- Sealing cuts off what comes from above. If the requested zone is a sealed zone or lies below one, an assignment made above that sealed zone does not cover it. Assignments made at the sealed zone or below it work as usual, and a sealed zone elsewhere in the tree has no effect.
- A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
- Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
- Decision: a request is allowed when some assignment that counts for the requester covers the requested zone with a role that allows the requested action. In every other case it is not allowed.

Penford Group - meeting rooms. Times are on the 24-hour clock. Confirmed bookings stay as they are. The request is confirmed unchanged or not at all, which needs every rule to hold for it.

== Booking rules ==
1. A booking must lie inside the opening hours of its room; it may start exactly at opening time and end exactly at closing time.
2. The request gives a start time and a duration; it ends at start + duration.
3. Some bookings repeat: a day field with several days separated by slashes means the booking exists on each of those days with the same room, time and people.
4. Two bookings of the same room need at least the reset gap of that room's kind between them, from the end of one to the start of the next; exactly the gap is enough. No gap is needed at opening or closing time.
5. What is booked on another day has no effect on the request.
6. A person, whether organiser or attendee, cannot be in two bookings that overlap in time on the same day, even in different rooms. People need no gap: one meeting may end at the very minute the person's next one starts.
7. Each item the request needs must be in the equipment list of the requested room itself; an item with a different name is a different item.
8. Everyone needs a seat: the organiser plus all attendees must not exceed the seats of the room. The organiser is never repeated among the attendees.
9. Two entries are the same person only if the full names are identical.

state:
Queue of: Kesimaro service desk, team 1
Clock at the moment of the decision: 17:20

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. A request that has waited at least 30 minutes moves up one class.
2. The flag "outage" moves a request up one class.
3. A request with a lower class number goes before a request with a higher class number.
4. Among requests of one class, a request with a due callback slot is ahead of a request without a due one.
5. If requests are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

How to read the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between requests that all rules before it leave level.
- Rules 1 and 2 do not order anything by themselves: they set the class that the later rules use.
- A request that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- Once moved, a request competes inside its new class on equal terms with the requests already there.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "logged" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- "At least 30 minutes" includes exactly 30 minutes; 29 minutes are not enough.
- Rules 1 and 2 do not add up: a request that meets both still moves up one class only.
- A callback slot counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The requests with a due callback slot are level with each other under this rule (the times under "callback" are not compared), and so are the requests without a due one.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting requests, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- Every request has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

Proposed install on daxtem-34, a field controller: the modules pinned at the end, taken from the module feed below.

Rules of this check:
- To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
- Bounds read as follows: >= at least, > strictly newer, <= at most, < strictly older, == exactly this version, != anything but this version; where several bounds follow one name, all of them apply.
- The set is clean only if the module feed lists every pinned version, every requirement of a pinned version is met by the pin of the required module, each runtime bound of a pinned version holds for the environment's runtime, and none of the pinned versions has a conflict entry that applies to another pin.
- Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the module feed says about other versions plays no part.
- Only pinned modules get installed; a required module that has no pin counts as unmet.
- Extra pins are fine: a pinned module that nothing requires is harmless as long as its own entry is satisfied.
- The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
- An entry 'cannot be combined with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about a module without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

Meaning of the fields:
- ticket: queue identifier of the task
- class: queue class, class 1 being the most urgent
- submitted: time the task was submitted (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the task; "-" means no marker
- reserved: time of the reserved start, "-" if there is none
- runtime: expected run time in minutes, whole minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Once the waiting time of a task is at least 50 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. Lower class number first.
3. Within the same class, tasks whose reserved start is due go first.
4. Lower ticket number first.

Notes on the rules:
- Read the rules from top to bottom; a later rule is used only to separate tasks that every earlier rule leaves level.
- Rule 1 does not order anything by itself: it sets the class that the later rules use.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- No task can go higher than class 1; a task of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- A task that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "submitted" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- "At least 50 minutes" includes exactly 50 minutes; 49 minutes are not enough.
- Due means that the time under "reserved" has been reached: it is equal to the current time or before it.
- Two tasks that are both due, or both not due (no reserved start, or one that is still to come), stay level under this rule.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two tasks have the same one.

state.policy:
Refund policy

General provisions
- In a conflict between rules, the earlier rule in the list prevails.
- By default a request is denied unless a rule says otherwise.

Rules
(1) When the time since purchase is under 30 days and the record shows yes for the proof of purchase flag: Approve the request.
(2) When the refund amount exceeds 300 EUR and the time since purchase is not below 30 days and the number of earlier refunds is at least 3: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(3) When the account age is lower than 14 days and the record shows yes for the fraud alert flag: Deny the request.
(4) When the time since purchase is greater than 21 days: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(5) When the account age is at least 120 days and the fraud alert flag is set to no: Approve the request.
(6) When the number of earlier refunds exceeds 4 and the refund amount is at least 1500 EUR: Deny the request.
(7) When the fraud alert flag is set to yes and the record shows no for the proof of purchase flag: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(8) When the time since purchase is 45 days or less and the number of earlier refunds is less than 2 and the record shows no for the fraud alert flag: Approve the request.
(9) When the fraud alert flag is set to yes and the number of earlier refunds is 4 or higher and the region is either Jordor or Yarvik: Deny the request.
(10) When the time since purchase is more than 21 days and the refund amount is at least 400 EUR: Deny the request.
(11) When the proof of purchase flag is no and the region is none of Galxan or Corwick and the refund amount is between 300 and 1500 EUR inclusive: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(12) When the case has the proof of purchase flag set to yes and the refund amount is below 200 EUR: Approve the request.

Exceptions
- Rule 8 is waived if the case has the proof of purchase flag set to no.
- Rule 9 is waived if the time since purchase is below 21 days.
- Rule 7 is waived if the refund amount is 400 EUR or less.
- Rule 4 is waived if the account age is 90 days or more and the case has the fraud alert flag set to no.

- The waiting time of a patient is counted in minutes from the time under "arrived" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- The limit itself counts: 75 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- Rank every waiting patient once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Every patient has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

state:
Access export of an invented records system. The rules in this export decide every request.

Request: user a.lirnoph asks to lookup at the section schools-west.

How access is decided:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- Assignments reach downward only: the section where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; sections beside it or above it are not.
- A sealed section blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher section covers neither the sealed section nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed section itself, or at a section below it, is not affected by that seal, and sections outside the sealed section are not affected either.
- Holding a role permits the actions on its own list and, when the role extends a second role, every action the second role permits (its own list and whatever it takes over by extension). The second role takes over nothing from the first.
- Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
- A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one section. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested section is the named section or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.
- Decision: a request is allowed when some assignment that counts for the requester covers the requested section with a role that allows the requested action, unless a deny entry applies. In every other case it is not allowed.

Refund policy

RULES
(1) When the number of earlier refunds is less than 1: Approve the request.
(2) When the refund amount is greater than 400 EUR and the number of earlier refunds is from 2 to 3 inclusive: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(3) When the number of earlier refunds is not more than 3 and the bank dispute flag is no and the fraud alert flag is no: Approve the request.
(4) When the region recorded for the case is Kelven and the fraud alert flag is set to yes: Deny the request.
(5) When the bank dispute flag is set to yes and the refund amount is greater than 300 EUR and the number of earlier refunds is 4 or more: Deny the request.
(6) When the region is among Stelbel or Yarkos and the record shows no for the bank dispute flag: Approve the request.
(7) When the fraud alert flag is set to yes and the case has the bank dispute flag set to yes: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
(8) When the number of earlier refunds is 3 or more and the region is among Kelven, Yarvik or Stelbel: Deny the request.

EXCEPTIONS
Exception to Rule 6: it is not applied when the number of earlier refunds exceeds 4.
Exception to Rule 1: it is not applied when the refund amount is above 400 EUR.
Exception to Rule 3: it is not applied when the refund amount is not below 400 EUR.

GENERAL
If two applicable rules lead to different outcomes, the lower-numbered rule decides.
When none of the rules applies, approve the request.

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Once the waiting time of a vessel is at least 30 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. A vessel with the flag "tidal" counts one class more urgent.
3. The vessels are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Of two vessels, the one with fewer minutes under "turnaround" is ahead.
5. If vessels are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Conventions:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- Rules 1 and 2 do not order anything by themselves: they set the class that the later rules use.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- No vessel can go higher than class 1; a vessel of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- After a class change a vessel is treated like every other vessel of its new class.
- Waiting time = current time minus the time under "anchored", in minutes (same day, 24-hour clock).
- A wait of exactly 30 minutes counts as at least 30 minutes.
- The two class changes are cumulative: meeting rule 1 and rule 2 means two classes up, with class 1 as the limit.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.

Expense approval rules

General provisions
- If two applicable rules lead to different outcomes, the higher-numbered rule decides.
- If no rule applies, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.

Rules
(1) If the case has the receipt attached flag set to no, the request is denied.
(2) If the time since the expense is above 30 days and the case has the duplicate suspicion flag set to yes, the request is denied.
(3) If the pre-approval flag is set to no and the grade is one of G5 or G2 and the time since the expense is 90 days or higher, the request is denied.
(4) If the time since the expense is 90 days or higher and the number of claims this quarter is between 3 and 5 inclusive, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.
(5) If the case has the duplicate suspicion flag set to no and the grade recorded for the case is G3, the request is approved.
(6) If the case has the duplicate suspicion flag set to no and the case has the receipt attached flag set to yes, the request is approved.
(7) If the claim amount is greater than 150 EUR, the request is denied.
(8) If the time since the expense is above 90 days and the record shows no for the receipt attached flag and the number of claims this quarter is more than 3, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.
(9) If the claim amount is at least 100 EUR and the time since the expense is above 30 days, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.
(10) If the duplicate suspicion flag is yes and the receipt attached flag is no, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.
(11) If the number of claims this quarter is at most 2 and the duplicate suspicion flag is no, the request is approved.
(12) If the record shows yes for the receipt attached flag and the grade is any of G2, G1 or G3, the request is approved.

Exceptions
- If the claim amount is above 500 EUR, Rule 12 does not apply.
- If the number of claims this quarter is lower than 3, Rule 2 does not apply.
- If the receipt attached flag is yes and the company card use flag is set to yes, Rule 9 does not apply.

Access export of an invented building access system. The rules in this export decide every request.

Access rules (they apply exactly as written):
1. An assignment gives one role to one user or to one group. An assignment to a group counts for every member of the group. Membership passes through nested groups: when group X is listed as a member of group Y, all members of X (also those X has through its own nested groups) are members of Y. It does not pass the other way: a user listed directly in Y is not thereby a member of X.
2. Assignments reach downward only: the zone where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; zones beside it or above it are not.
3. Exception for sealed zones: an assignment never passes into a sealed zone from a zone above it, so the sealed zone and everything below it stay out of its reach. A seal does nothing to an assignment made at the sealed zone or below it, and nothing to zones that are not inside the sealed zone.
4. Holding a role permits the actions on its own list and, when the role extends a second role, every action the second role permits (its own list and whatever it takes over by extension). The second role takes over nothing from the first.
5. Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
6. A deny entry forbids one action to one user, or to all direct and nested members of one group, on one zone and all zones below it; seals make no difference to deny entries. When an entry matches the requester, the exact action and the zone, the request is refused whatever the assignments say. An entry for a different action never matches, and inclusions between actions are ignored for deny entries.
7. A request is allowed if at least one assignment gives the requester a role that allows the requested action and covers the requested zone, and no deny entry applies. Otherwise it is not allowed.

How the two ledgers are matched:
Rule 1: An entry of A and a line of B belong together when their doc number values are identical, character for character.
Rule 2: Lines in B are not sorted the way A is; their position tells nothing.
Rule 3: B may hold extra lines whose doc number matches nothing in A (no entry, no payment run number); they play no part.

Rule 7: Two B lines with the same doc number stand for one entry of A; the entry reconciles when their sum equals its amount multiplied by -1 and neither line breaks the date rule.
Rule 8: Entries of A with method WIRE reach B less a transfer charge of 1.50 each: the amount figure on the B line is 1.50 smaller in size than the amount figure in A (the size of a figure is its value without the sign), and its sign is reversed. Permission data of a fictional records system, followed by the rules that govern it.

The request: may user t.lirverd export in the section leases?

How access is decided:
1. An assignment gives one role to one user or to one group. An assignment to a group counts for every member of the group. Membership passes through nested groups: when group X is listed as a member of group Y, all members of X (also those X has through its own nested groups) are members of Y. It does not pass the other way: a user listed directly in Y is not thereby a member of X.
2. Assignments reach downward only: the section where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; sections beside it or above it are not.
3. Sealing cuts off what comes from above. If the requested section is a sealed section or lies below one, an assignment made above that sealed section does not cover it. Assignments made at the sealed section or below it work as usual, and a sealed section elsewhere in the tree has no effect.
4. Holding a role permits the actions on its own list and, when the role extends a second role, every action the second role permits (its own list and whatever it takes over by extension). The second role takes over nothing from the first.
5. Where the inclusion list states that one action includes another, permission for the first counts as permission for the second, and likewise onward along several such lines. There are no unlisted inclusions, and the included action never brings the including one.
6. Deny entries win over assignments. An entry blocks its action for the user it names, or for every member of the group it names (members through nested groups included), on its section and on everything below that section, sealed or not. It blocks that single action only; requests for other actions are judged as if the entry were not there, also when the actions are linked by an inclusion.
7. A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested section and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.

How access is decided:
1. A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
2. The role of an assignment is valid on the collection named in the assignment and on all collections below that collection at any depth, not on any other collection.
3. A sealed collection blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher collection covers neither the sealed collection nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed collection itself, or at a collection below it, is not affected by that seal, and collections outside the sealed collection are not affected either.
4. Holding a role permits the actions on its own list and, when the role extends a second role, every action the second role permits (its own list and whatever it takes over by extension). The second role takes over nothing from the first.
5. The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
6. A deny entry forbids one action to one user, or to all direct and nested members of one group, on one collection and all collections below it; seals make no difference to deny entries. When an entry matches the requester, the exact action and the collection, the request is refused whatever the assignments say. An entry for a different action never matches, and inclusions between actions are ignored for deny entries.
7. A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested collection and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.

Rules of this check:
- To order two versions, compare the first numbers, then the second, then the third, always as whole numbers, so 0.10.1 comes after 0.9.8 and 1.2.10 after 1.2.9. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
- Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
- A clean install needs all of the following: each pin is a version that the module feed lists; for each pinned version, each module it requires is pinned too, at a version inside the stated bounds; the runtime of the environment satisfies the runtime bounds of all pinned versions; no pinned version has a 'cannot be combined with' entry that applies to another pin.
- Entries of versions that are not pinned are irrelevant.
- Only pinned modules get installed; a required module that has no pin counts as unmet.
- A pin that no pinned version requires does no harm by itself; its own entry is checked like that of every other pin.
- The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).
- An entry 'cannot be combined with P B' under a pinned version means that the set fails when P is pinned at a version meeting the bound B; it does not matter which of the two lists it, and an entry about a module without a pin, or whose pin misses B, does no harm.

state.policy:
Refund approval policy

General provisions
- When rules conflict, the rule with the higher number wins.
- A request that no rule covers is escalated to a human reviewer.

Rules
Rule 1. When the refund amount is 500 EUR or more: Deny the request.
Rule 2. When the time since purchase is 21 days or higher and the case has the item returned flag set to no: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 3. When the time since purchase is under 21 days and the refund amount is below 200 EUR: Approve the request.
Rule 4. When the fraud alert flag is yes and the time since purchase is above 45 days: Deny the request.
Rule 5. When the time since purchase lies in the range 21 to 30 days inclusive and the bank dispute flag is yes: Deny the request.
Rule 6. When the refund amount is from 500 to 1500 EUR inclusive: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 7. When the record shows no for the bank dispute flag and the account age exceeds 120 days: Approve the request.
Rule 8. When the case has the fraud alert flag set to no: Approve the request.
Rule 9. When the item returned flag is yes: Approve the request.
Rule 10. When the record shows no for the proof of purchase flag and the record shows yes for the fraud alert flag and the refund amount is at least 300 EUR: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 11. When the proof of purchase flag is set to no and the case has the item returned flag set to no: Deny the request.
Rule 12. When the region on record is Dovtor and the time since purchase is more than 60 days: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.

Exceptions
- Rule 12 does not apply when the refund amount is below 500 EUR.
- Rule 10 does not apply when the account age is above 270 days.
- Rule 3 does not apply when the account age is under 14 days.

How access is decided:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- The role of an assignment is valid on the zone named in the assignment and on all zones below that zone at any depth, not on any other zone.
- Exception for sealed zones: an assignment never passes into a sealed zone from a zone above it, so the sealed zone and everything below it stay out of its reach. A seal does nothing to an assignment made at the sealed zone or below it, and nothing to zones that are not inside the sealed zone.
- The actions a role allows are its own actions plus the actions of the role it extends, plus those of the role that one extends, and so on. Nothing is passed in the opposite direction, from the extending role to the extended one.
- The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
- A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one zone. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested zone is the named zone or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.
- A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested zone and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.
