- logged: time the request was logged, as HH:MM on today's 24-hour clock
- flag: at most one marker per request ("-" = none)
- callback: time of the agreed callback; "-" means none
- effort: estimated effort in minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 35 minutes lifts a request by one class.
2. Lower class number first.
3. Earlier logging time first.
4. If requests are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Conventions:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- Rule 1 changes the class of a request and is applied to every request before anything is compared; in the rules after it, "class" means the class after this change.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- Class 1 is the top: a request never moves above class 1.
- After a class change a request is treated like every other request of its new class.
- The waiting time of a request is counted in minutes from the time under "logged" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- The limit itself counts: 35 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting requests, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Ticket numbers are the digits after the dash, compared as numbers, and they are unique.

What the list shows:
- ticket: the code under which the vessel is queued
- class: berth class, class 1 being the most urgent
- anchored: time the vessel dropped anchor (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the vessel; "-" means no marker
- window: start of the booked berth window, "-" if there is none
- turnaround: the expected turnaround time in minutes

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 40 minutes lifts a vessel by one class.
2. Any vessel carrying the flag "reefer" is lifted by one class.
3. The vessels are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Of two vessels, the one with fewer minutes under "turnaround" is ahead.
5. Earlier anchoring time first.
6. If vessels are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Notes on the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between vessels that all rules before it leave level.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each vessel; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- A vessel that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- Once moved, a vessel competes inside its new class on equal terms with the vessels already there.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "anchored" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- "At least 40 minutes" includes exactly 40 minutes; 39 minutes are not enough.
- Rules 1 and 2 do not add up: a vessel that meets both still moves up one class only.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- Every vessel has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

Wanted: the vessel standing first in the order worked out at the current time

Rule 12. A request for which the tenure is at most 365 days and the clearance level is within 2 to 3 with both limits included is escalated to a human reviewer.

- window: start of the booked berth window ("-" = none)
- turnaround: the expected turnaround time in minutes

Ordering rules (apply them in this order):
1. Once the waiting time of a vessel is at least 35 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. Any vessel carrying the flag "tidal" is lifted by one class.
3. The vessels are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Among vessels of one class, a vessel with a due berth window is ahead of a vessel without a due one.
5. The vessel that anchored earlier goes first.
6. Lower ticket number first.

How to read the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each vessel; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- After a class change a vessel is treated like every other vessel of its new class.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "anchored" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- The limit itself counts: 35 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- The two class changes are cumulative: meeting rule 1 and rule 2 means two classes up, with class 1 as the limit.
- A berth window counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the berth window was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two vessels have the same one.

The request: may user a.grivregh archive in the folder legal?

How access is decided:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- An assignment is made at one folder. It covers that folder and every folder below it (directly or further down), and nothing else.
- A sealed folder blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher folder covers neither the sealed folder nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed folder itself, or at a folder below it, is not affected by that seal, and folders outside the sealed folder are not affected either.
- The actions a role allows are its own actions plus the actions of the role it extends, plus those of the role that one extends, and so on. Nothing is passed in the opposite direction, from the extending role to the extended one.
- Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
- A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one folder. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested folder is the named folder or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.
- Decision: a request is allowed when some assignment that counts for the requester covers the requested folder with a role that allows the requested action, unless a deny entry applies. In every other case it is not allowed.

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 20 minutes lifts a patient by one class.

- The waiting time of a patient is counted in minutes from the time under "arrived" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- The limit itself counts: 20 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- A patient moves up at most one class in total, even when both rule 1 and rule 2 apply to it.

Expense approval rules

General provisions
- When rules conflict, the rule with the lower number wins.
- When none of the rules applies, approve the request.

Rules
(1) A request for which the receipt attached flag is set to no is escalated to a human reviewer.
(2) A request for which the time since the expense is greater than 60 days and the number of claims this quarter is from 5 to 8 inclusive is escalated to a human reviewer.
(3) A request for which the claim amount lies in the range 250 to 500 EUR inclusive and the duplicate suspicion flag is yes is denied.
(4) A request for which the time since the expense is at least 90 days and the number of claims this quarter is more than 5 and the claim amount is not below 100 EUR is escalated to a human reviewer.
(5) A request for which the grade recorded for the case is G2 and the claim amount is at least 100 EUR is denied.
(6) A request for which the grade is not G1 and the record shows yes for the receipt attached flag is approved.
(7) A request for which the duplicate suspicion flag is set to no is approved.
(8) A request for which the claim amount does not exceed 50 EUR and the grade is not among G4 or G3 is approved.
(9) A request for which the duplicate suspicion flag is yes and the number of claims this quarter is greater than 3 is escalated to a human reviewer.
(10) A request for which the claim amount is below 250 EUR and the time since the expense is at most 30 days is approved.
(11) A request for which the grade is any of G1, G3 or G5 and the time since the expense is 45 days or higher is denied.
(12) A request for which the number of claims this quarter is 8 or more and the cost centre is not CC-455 is denied.

Exceptions
- Rule 11 is waived if the receipt attached flag is set to yes and the claim amount is under 100 EUR.
- Rule 2 is waived if the claim amount is not more than 500 EUR.
- Rule 9 is waived if the time since the expense is at most 30 days and the cost centre recorded for the case is CC-512.

state:
Period under review: August 2026. Ledger A is the timesheet of the Selvolm team, and ledger B is the client hours log signed off by Hoskand Ceramics.

Conventions for this reconciliation:
Rule 1: Each entry of A is matched only with the lines of B that carry exactly the same sheet id.
Rule 2: B is kept by the other side, so every hours figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
Rule 3: An entry of A is in order when its B line shows the same size of hours figure with the opposite sign, inside the date tolerance. Exceptions follow below for split entries, for mode TRAVEL and for entries with a roll-up number.
Rule 4: Dates may differ by at most 2 days in either direction; a gap of exactly 2 days is still accepted, a larger one is not.
Rule 5: Two B lines with the same sheet id stand for one entry of A; the entry reconciles when their sum equals its hours multiplied by -1 and neither line breaks the date rule.
Rule 6: A line for an entry with mode TRAVEL is 0.50 h smaller in size in B (travel deduction; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 0.50 h in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 0.50 h. Other mode values carry no deduction.
Rule 7: B combines the A entries of one roll-up number into one line with that number as sheet id and their summed hours, sign reversed; their own sheet id values do not appear in B, and the line must be within the date tolerance of their common date.
Rule 8: A combined line that is short by the exact hours of one of its entries means that this one entry is missing from it and does not reconcile, while the rest of the roll-up is fine.
Rule 9: Lines in B are not sorted the way A is; their position tells nothing.
Rule 10: A line of B that carries no sheet id and no roll-up number of A is left aside; it affects no entry.

state:
Reconciliation for April 2025. Ledger A is the cash book of Hoskevi Instruments; ledger B is the bank statement issued by Bank of Yorvada.

Conventions for this reconciliation:
Rule 1: An entry of A and a line of B belong together when their reference values are identical, character for character.
Rule 2: All amount figures in B carry the sign opposite to the one in A.
Rule 3: An entry of A is in order when its B line shows the same size of amount figure with the opposite sign, inside the date tolerance. Exceptions follow below for split entries, for channel CARD and for entries with a lodgement number.
Rule 4: The date of a B line may be up to 5 days earlier or later than the date of its A entry; a gap of more than 5 days means the entry does not reconcile.
Rule 5: Two B lines with the same reference stand for one entry of A; the entry reconciles when their sum equals its amount multiplied by -1 and neither line breaks the date rule.
Rule 6: A line for an entry with channel CARD is 0.15 smaller in size in B (processing fee; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 0.15 in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 0.15. Other channel values carry no deduction.
Rule 7: B combines the A entries of one lodgement number into one line with that number as reference and their summed amount, sign reversed; their own reference values do not appear in B, and the line must be within the date tolerance of their common date.
Rule 8: When a combined line is smaller in size than the total by precisely the amount of one of its entries, only that entry fails to reconcile.
Rule 9: Lines in B are not sorted the way A is; their position tells nothing.
Rule 10: A line of B that carries no reference and no lodgement number of A is left aside; it affects no entry.

state:
Reconciliation for March 2025. Ledger A is the stock system in which the Selvora store books its movements; ledger B is the receiving log kept at the Mernolm depot.

Matching conventions:
1. Each entry of A is matched only with the lines of B that carry exactly the same movement id.
2. The order of the lines in B carries no meaning and differs from the order of A.
3. Lines of B whose movement id is neither a movement id of A nor a pallet number of A relate to other business and are ignored.
4. B is kept by the other side, so every quantity figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
5. An entry reconciles when the quantity figure on its B line is its own quantity figure with the sign reversed and the date rule holds. Split entries, entries with route SAMPLE and entries with a pallet number follow their own rules below.
6. Dates may differ by at most 3 days in either direction; a gap of exactly 3 days is still accepted, a larger one is not.
7. B sometimes splits one entry into two lines with the same movement id; together they must give the entry's quantity with the opposite sign, and each line must be inside the date tolerance.
8. Entries of A with route SAMPLE reach B less a retained test sample of 2 units each: the quantity figure on the B line is 2 units smaller in size than the quantity figure in A (the size of a figure is its value without the sign), and its sign is reversed. This holds for plus and minus figures alike. No other route has a deduction.
9. Entries of A that share a pallet number appear in B as one line whose movement id is that number and whose quantity figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.
10. A combined line that is short by the exact quantity of one of its entries means that this one entry is missing from it and does not reconcile, while the rest of the pallet is fine.

At most one entry of A fails to reconcile.

Request: user r.vespack asks to transfer at the section complaints.

Rules:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- Assignments reach downward only: the section where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; sections beside it or above it are not.
- A sealed section blocks assignments from above: an assignment made at a higher section covers neither the sealed section nor anything below it. An assignment made at the sealed section itself, or at a section below it, is not affected by that seal, and sections outside the sealed section are not affected either.
- A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
- The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
- A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one section. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested section is the named section or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.
- A request is allowed only when an assignment whose role the requester holds covers the requested section and that role allows the requested action; in addition no deny entry may apply.

Rules:
1. Each assignment names a role and either a user or a group; if it names a group, every member of the group holds the role. Groups may list other groups as members. A user belongs to a group if the group lists the user or lists a group the user belongs to, over any number of steps. Belonging never runs downward: the users listed in an outer group do not belong to the groups listed inside it.
2. An assignment is made at one namespace. It covers that namespace and every namespace below it (directly or further down), and nothing else.
3. Exception for sealed namespaces: an assignment never passes into a sealed namespace from a namespace above it, so the sealed namespace and everything below it stay out of its reach. A seal does nothing to an assignment made at the sealed namespace or below it, and nothing to namespaces that are not inside the sealed namespace.
4. The actions a role allows are its own actions plus the actions of the role it extends, plus those of the role that one extends, and so on. Nothing is passed in the opposite direction, from the extending role to the extended one.
5. The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
6. A deny entry forbids one action to one user, or to all direct and nested members of one group, on one namespace and all namespaces below it; seals make no difference to deny entries. How access is decided:
- A role is held by the user an assignment names or, when it names a group, by every member of that group. The members of a group are the users on its list plus all members of each group on its list, and so on through further nesting. A group that is nested inside another gains no members from the group that contains it.
- Assignments reach downward only: the section where an assignment is made and everything below it, however deep, are covered; sections beside it or above it are not.
- Exception for sealed sections: an assignment never passes into a sealed section from a section above it, so the sealed section and everything below it stay out of its reach. A seal does nothing to an assignment made at the sealed section or below it, and nothing to sections that are not inside the sealed section.
- Holding a role permits the actions on its own list and, when the role extends a second role, every action the second role permits (its own list and whatever it takes over by extension). The second role takes over nothing from the first.
- Actions can include other actions, exactly as listed. Being allowed an action means being allowed every action it includes, directly or through a chain of listed inclusions. An inclusion is never read backwards, and actions without a listed link do not include each other.
- A deny entry names a user or a group, one action and one section. It applies to a request when the requester is that user or a member of that group (nested membership counts), the requested action is exactly the named action, and the requested section is the named section or lies below it; a seal does not stop a deny entry. A deny entry that applies beats every assignment. It affects no other action: denying X does not block Y, even if X includes Y or Y includes X.

state:
Location: Rudivar port control, berth desk 9
Clock at the moment of the decision: 15:10

Ordering rules (apply them in this order):
1. Waiting at least 75 minutes lifts a vessel by one class.
2. A vessel with the flag "reefer" counts one class more urgent.
3. Lower class number first.
4. Within the same class, vessels whose berth window is due go first.
5. If vessels are still level, the lower ticket number is ahead.

Conventions:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between vessels that all rules before it leave level.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each vessel; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- No vessel can go higher than class 1; a vessel of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- A vessel that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- The waiting time of a vessel is counted in minutes from the time under "anchored" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- "At least 75 minutes" includes exactly 75 minutes; 74 minutes are not enough.
- Both class changes can apply to the same vessel; it then moves up two classes in total, stopping at class 1.
- Due means that the time under "window" has been reached: it is equal to the current time or before it.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the berth window was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- Rank every waiting vessel once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Every vessel has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

- The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
- A deny entry forbids one action to one user, or to all direct and nested members of one group, on one folder and all folders below it; seals make no difference to deny entries. When an entry matches the requester, the exact action and the folder, the request is refused whatever the assignments say. Meaning of the fields:
- ticket: queue identifier of the patient
- class: triage class; a smaller number means more urgent
- arrived: time the patient arrived, as HH:MM on today's 24-hour clock
- flag: marker of the patient, "-" if none
- slot: time of the booked slot, "-" if there is none
- consult: expected consultation time in minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Once the waiting time of a patient is at least 60 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. A patient with a lower class number goes before a patient with a higher class number.
3. Inside a class, every patient whose booked slot is due precedes every patient whose booked slot is not due.
4. Last tie-break: the patient with the lower ticket number goes first.

Conventions:
- Read the rules from top to bottom; a later rule is used only to separate patients that every earlier rule leaves level.
- Rule 1 changes the class of a patient and is applied to every patient before anything is compared; in the rules after it, "class" means the class after this change.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- Class 1 is the top: a patient never moves above class 1.
- Once moved, a patient competes inside its new class on equal terms with the patients already there.
- Waiting time = current time minus the time under "arrived", in minutes (same day, 24-hour clock).
- "At least 60 minutes" includes exactly 60 minutes; 59 minutes are not enough.
- Due means that the time under "slot" has been reached: it is equal to the current time or before it.
- The rule only separates due from not due: how early the booked slot was does not matter, and "-" or a later time counts as not due.
- Rank every waiting patient once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Every patient has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

Asked: the patient that is first in the order

state:
Queue of: Lunettra cycle and tool repairs, service bench 2
Clock at the moment of the decision: 12:18

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. A job that has waited at least 35 minutes moves up one class.
2. A job with the flag "safety" counts one class more urgent.
3. A job with a lower class number goes before a job with a higher class number.
4. Among jobs of one class, a job with a due pickup time is ahead of a job without a due one.
5. Earlier check-in first.
6. Lower ticket number first.

Notes on the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- Rules 1 and 2 change the class of a job and are applied to every job before anything is compared; in the rules after them, "class" means the class after these changes.
- A job that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- No job can go higher than class 1; a job of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- A job that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- The waiting time of a job is counted in minutes from the time under "checkin" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- "At least 35 minutes" includes exactly 35 minutes; 34 minutes are not enough.
- A job moves up at most one class in total, even when both rule 1 and rule 2 apply to it.
- A pickup time counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The jobs with a due pickup time are level with each other under this rule (the times under "pickup" are not compared), and so are the jobs without a due one.
- The order is worked out once, for all waiting jobs, at the current time; first, second and third are positions in this one order.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two jobs have the same one.

Expense claim handling

(5) If the claim amount exceeds 1000 EUR and the number of claims this quarter is at least 8, the request is escalated to a human reviewer.

state:
Permission data of a fictional document workspace, followed by the rules that govern it.

How access is decided:
- Each assignment names a role and either a user or a group; if it names a group, every member of the group holds the role. Groups may list other groups as members. A user belongs to a group if the group lists the user or lists a group the user belongs to, over any number of steps. Belonging never runs downward: the users listed in an outer group do not belong to the groups listed inside it.
- An assignment is made at one folder. It covers that folder and every folder below it (directly or further down), and nothing else.
- Sealing cuts off what comes from above. If the requested folder is a sealed folder or lies below one, an assignment made above that sealed folder does not cover it. Assignments made at the sealed folder or below it work as usual, and a sealed folder elsewhere in the tree has no effect.
- A role allows the actions listed for it. A role that extends another role also allows everything the other role allows, including what that role gets from a role it extends. Extension works one way only: the extended role gains nothing.
- The inclusion list says which action includes which. If X includes Y, a role that allows X allows Y as well; inclusions chain, so if Y in turn includes Z, then X includes Z. Only the listed inclusions exist, and none works in reverse.
- A deny entry forbids one action to one user, or to all direct and nested members of one group, on one folder and all folders below it; seals make no difference to deny entries. When an entry matches the requester, the exact action and the folder, the request is refused whatever the assignments say. An entry for a different action never matches, and inclusions between actions are ignored for deny entries.
- A request is allowed if at least one assignment gives the requester a role that allows the requested action and covers the requested folder, and no deny entry applies. Otherwise it is not allowed.

Known actions: view | comment | export | edit | archive

Listed inclusions (only these exist):
inclusion: export includes comment
inclusion: edit includes view
inclusion: edit includes comment
inclusion: archive includes comment

Proposed install on tavilo-41, a pipeline runner: the plugins pinned at the end, taken from the plugin registry below.

How to read the entries and when a set is clean:
1. Versions are ordered part by part as integers, not as text: 3.10.0 is later than 3.9.9, and 2.0.0 is later than 1.15.2. The same holds for the two-part runtime versions: 2.10 comes after 2.9.
2. Each bound is an operator and a version: >= (that version or newer), > (newer only), <= (that version or older), < (older only), == (only that version), != (every version but that one); a list of bounds is met only when each bound is met.
3. The proposed set installs cleanly when every pinned version is listed in the plugin registry, every requirement of every pinned version names a plugin that is pinned at a version meeting all of its bounds, and the runtime of the target environment meets every runtime bound of every pinned version.
4. Only the entries of the pinned versions count; what the plugin registry says about other versions plays no part.
5. Only pinned plugins get installed; a required plugin that has no pin counts as unmet.
6. Pinning a plugin that nothing needs is allowed, but the entry of that pinned version must still be met.
7. The environment's runtime must satisfy each runtime bound of each pinned version ('any' means no bound).

state:
Parties: Neltivo Partners ("the Manufacturer") and Jorvesk Group ("the Distributor"). Document: Distribution agreement, in two versions (A and B), with a case at the end.
Conventions:
- The case is to be decided twice: under version A as if it were the only text, and under version B as if it were the only text.
- The numbering can shift from one version to the other when a clause is moved or added, so clauses correspond by subject and not by number.
- The condition written in a clause is complete: if it is met, what the clause provides applies, and if it is not met, it does not apply.
- Limits are literal. The stated figure itself satisfies a limit worded with "at least", "at most", "no more than", "no fewer than", "no less than", "no later than", "or more", "or fewer" or "or less"; it does not satisfy a limit worded with "more than", "fewer than", "less than", "over", "under" or "below".
- Each point at issue and each condition of a request depends on one clause, the one on its subject; other facts of the case leave it untouched.
[Version A]
1. Cooperation. The parties cooperate in good faith and share the information needed to perform this agreement.
2. Insurance. The Manufacturer keeps adequate insurance cover for its activities under this agreement.
3. Warranty. Warranty cover applies to a defect that is reported at most 27 months after delivery.
4. Unforeseeable events. Neither party is in breach while an event beyond its reasonable control prevents performance.
5. Disputes. The parties try to settle any dispute by talks between their managers before taking any further step.
6. Termination. Either party may end this agreement by written notice given over 25 days before the intended end date.
7. Late delivery. An order may be cancelled by the Distributor once its delivery is late by more than 9 days.
8. Deposit. The Manufacturer is bound by an order when it has received a deposit of 32 percent or more of the order value.
9. Entire agreement. This agreement replaces all earlier arrangements between the parties on the same subject.
10. Service credits. A service credit is due for a calendar month in which the dealer portal is unavailable for over 19 hours.
11. Response time. The Manufacturer meets the response time when it answers a dealer query under 47 hours after receipt.
12. Liability. A claim for damages against the Manufacturer is payable in full when the amount claimed is 26500 krevs or less.
[Version B]
1. Insurance. The Manufacturer keeps adequate insurance cover for its activities under this agreement.

Reconciliation for September 2025. Ledger A is the dispatch register of the Coskand plant; ledger B is the weighbridge record of the haulier Tarnevi Haulage.

Matching conventions:
1. Pairing goes by note id alone: an entry of A goes with the B line or lines showing the very same note id.
2. B is kept by the other side, so every weight figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
3. A pair agrees when the B weight figure equals the A weight figure multiplied by -1 and the dates are within the tolerance. The rules below cover the exceptions: split entries, packing PALLET entries and load entries.

7. Entries of A that share a load number appear in B as one line whose note id is that number and whose weight figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.

9. B lists its lines in its own order, not in the order of A.

Rule 2. A request for which the number of claims this quarter is not below 8 and the receipt attached flag is no and the time since the expense is more than 30 days is denied.
Rule 3. A request for which the case has the receipt attached flag set to yes and the grade is none of G3, G1 or G2 is approved.

Rule 8. A request for which the grade is either G1 or G4 and the claim amount is from 1000 to 2000 EUR inclusive is escalated to a human reviewer.
Rule 9. A request for which the grade is one of G5 or G1 and the time since the expense is between 60 and 90 days inclusive is denied.
Rule 10. A request for which the time since the expense is under 14 days is approved.
Rule 11. A request for which the number of claims this quarter is less than 2 and the record shows yes for the receipt attached flag and the case has the company card use flag set to yes is approved.
Rule 12. A request for which the cost centre is any of CC-204, CC-117 or CC-512 and the claim amount is at least 100 EUR is denied.

Exceptions:

- If the case has the company card use flag set to yes, Rule 8 does not apply.

q.instructions: Which entry of ledger A does not reconcile with ledger B?

state:
Reconciliation for July 2025. Ledger A is the stock system of the Dulvela store; ledger B is the receiving log of the Quorik depot.

Matching conventions:
(1) Each entry of A is matched only with the lines of B that carry exactly the same movement id.
(2) Signs are mirrored between the two ledgers: what is positive in A is negative in B, and what is negative in A is positive in B.
(3) A pair agrees when the B quantity figure equals the A quantity figure multiplied by -1 and the dates are within the tolerance. The rules below cover the exceptions: split entries, route SAMPLE entries and pallet entries.
(4) The date of a B line may be up to 1 day earlier or later than the date of its A entry; a gap of more than 1 day means the entry does not reconcile.
(5) B sometimes splits one entry into two lines with the same movement id; together they must give the entry's quantity with the opposite sign, and each line must be inside the date tolerance.
(6) A line for an entry with route SAMPLE is 1 units smaller in size in B (retained test sample; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 1 units in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 1 units. Other route values carry no deduction.
(7) B combines the A entries of one pallet number into one line with that number as movement id and their summed quantity, sign reversed; their own movement id values do not appear in B, and the line must be within the date tolerance of their common date.
(8) When a combined line is smaller in size than the total by precisely the quantity of one of its entries, only that entry fails to reconcile.
(9) The order of the lines in B carries no meaning and differs from the order of A.
(10) B may hold extra lines whose movement id matches nothing in A (no entry, no pallet number); they play no part.

No more than one entry of A can fail; possibly none does.

Meaning of the fields:
- ticket: identifier of the task
- class: the queue class (1 = most urgent)
- submitted: time the task was submitted; all times are today's, 24-hour clock
- flag: a marker noted for the task; "-" means no marker
- reserved: time of the reserved start; "-" means none
- runtime: the expected run time in minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 75 minutes lifts a task by one class.
2. Any task carrying the flag "review" is lifted by one class.
3. The tasks are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Of two tasks, the one with fewer minutes under "runtime" is ahead.
5. Of two tasks, the one with the earlier time under "submitted" is ahead.
6. Last tie-break: the task with the lower ticket number goes first.

How to read the rules:
- An earlier rule always outranks a later one; a later rule only breaks ties that remain after the rules above it.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each task; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- Moving up one class means that the class number becomes one smaller (class 3 becomes class 2).
- Class 1 is the top: a task never moves above class 1.
- A task that has moved up is an ordinary member of its new class; nothing else about it changes.
- The waiting time of a task is counted in minutes from the time under "submitted" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- The limit itself counts: 75 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- The two class changes are not cumulative: meeting rule 1 and rule 2 counts the same as meeting one of them.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Whatever the list shows that no rule uses (a column, a flag) is for information only.
- Ticket numbers are the digits after the dash, compared as numbers, and they are unique.

Wanted: the task standing second in the order worked out at the current time

Data export policy

General provisions
- Conflicting rules are resolved in favour of the rule with the larger number.
- When none of the rules applies, escalate the request to a human reviewer.

Rules
(1) The request must be approved if the account age is 365 days or higher and the export size is under 100 records.
(2) The request must be approved if the consent on file flag is yes and the account age is at least 90 days.
(3) The request must be escalated to a human reviewer if the number of exports in the last 30 days is more than 2 and the data region recorded for the case is Zanfen.
(4) The request must be denied if the account age is less than 180 days and the data region is either Quilnex or Zanfen and the consent on file flag is no.
(5) The request must be approved if the verified requester flag is yes and the number of exports in the last 30 days is lower than 2.
(6) The request must be escalated to a human reviewer if the record shows no for the consent on file flag and the number of exports in the last 30 days is at least 3.
(7) The request must be approved if the case has the verified requester flag set to yes and the account age is greater than 180 days.
(8) The request must be denied if the verified requester flag is no and the number of exports in the last 30 days is not below 3.
(9) The request must be escalated to a human reviewer if the export size is not below 10000 records.
(10) The request must be escalated to a human reviewer if the case has the verified requester flag set to no and the consent on file flag is no.
(11) The request must be denied if the record shows no for the consent on file flag and the export size is at least 50000 records.
(12) The request must be denied if the record shows no for the consent on file flag and the case has the verified requester flag set to no.

Exceptions
- Rule 4 does not apply when the number of exports in the last 30 days is less than 3 and the export size is below 5000 records.
- Rule 12 does not apply when the account age is greater than 90 days.
- Rule 7 does not apply when the number of exports in the last 30 days is more than 3 and the export size is more than 1000 records.

Rule 9: Entries of A that share a load number appear in B as one line whose note id is that number and whose weight figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.

Fields of the list:

- arrived: time the patient arrived (today, 24-hour clock)
- flag: a marker noted for the patient; "-" means no marker
- slot: time of the booked slot, "-" if there is none
- consult: expected consultation time in minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Waiting at least 25 minutes lifts a patient by one class.
2. Any patient carrying the flag "infant" is lifted by one class.
3. The patients are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Inside a class, every patient whose booked slot is due precedes every patient whose booked slot is not due.
5. Lower ticket number first.

Notes on the rules:
- Read the rules from top to bottom; a later rule is used only to separate patients that every earlier rule leaves level.
- Rules 1 and 2 do not order anything by themselves: they set the class that the later rules use.
- A patient that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- No patient can go higher than class 1; a patient of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- After a class change a patient is treated like every other patient of its new class.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "arrived" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- A wait of exactly 25 minutes counts as at least 25 minutes.
- Both class changes can apply to the same patient; it then moves up two classes in total, stopping at class 1.
- A booked slot counts as due from its own minute on, that is, when it is not later than the current time.
- The patients with a due booked slot are level with each other under this rule (the times under "slot" are not compared), and so are the patients without a due one.
- Rank every waiting patient once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- Every patient has its own ticket number: the number that follows the dash in the identifier.

Asked: the patient that is first in the order

4. B is kept by the other side, so every quantity figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
5. An entry reconciles when the quantity figure on its B line is its own quantity figure with the sign reversed and the date rule holds. Split entries, entries with route SAMPLE and entries with a pallet number follow their own rules below.
6. Dates may differ by at most 3 days in either direction; a gap of exactly 3 days is still accepted, a larger one is not.
7. B sometimes splits one entry into two lines with the same movement id; together they must give the entry's quantity with the opposite sign, and each line must be inside the date tolerance.
8. Entries of A with route SAMPLE reach B less a retained test sample of 2 units each: the quantity figure on the B line is 2 units smaller in size than the quantity figure in A (the size of a figure is its value without the sign), and its sign is reversed. This holds for plus and minus figures alike. No other route has a deduction.
9. Entries of A that share a pallet number appear in B as one line whose movement id is that number and whose quantity figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.
10. A combined line that is short by the exact quantity of one of its entries means that this one entry is missing from it and does not reconcile, while the rest of the pallet is fine.

Fields of the list:

- class: urgency class; a smaller number means more urgent

- flag: marker of the job, "-" if none
- pickup: time of the agreed pickup ("-" = none)
- bench: expected bench time in minutes

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. A job that has waited at least 75 minutes moves up one class.
2. The flag "courier" moves a job up one class.
3. A job with a lower class number goes before a job with a higher class number.
4. The job that was checked in earlier goes first.
5. The job with the shorter bench time goes first.
6. Last tie-break: the job with the lower ticket number goes first.

How to read the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between jobs that all rules before it leave level.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each job; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- "Up one class" is the class number minus 1; for example, class 4 turns into class 3.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- After a class change a job is treated like every other job of its new class.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "checkin" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- "At least 75 minutes" includes exactly 75 minutes; 74 minutes are not enough.
- The two class changes are cumulative: meeting rule 1 and rule 2 means two classes up, with class 1 as the limit.
- Rank every waiting job once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two jobs have the same one.

Wanted: the job standing first in the order worked out at the current time

state:

Conventions for this reconciliation:
1. An entry of A and a line of B belong together when their movement id values are identical, character for character.

3. Lines of B whose movement id is neither a movement id of A nor a pallet number of A relate to other business and are ignored.
4. B is kept by the other side, so every quantity figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
5. A pair agrees when the B quantity figure equals the A quantity figure multiplied by -1 and the dates are within the tolerance. The rules below cover the exceptions: split entries, route SAMPLE entries and pallet entries.
6. A B line dated more than 5 days before or after its A entry is not a valid match, so that entry does not reconcile; 5 days or less is fine.
7. Two B lines with the same movement id stand for one entry of A; the entry reconciles when their sum equals its quantity multiplied by -1 and neither line breaks the date rule.
8. A line for an entry with route SAMPLE is 4 units smaller in size in B (retained test sample; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 4 units in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 4 units. Rule 7: Entries of A that share a load number appear in B as one line whose note id is that number and whose weight figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.

state.policy:
Refund approval policy

General provisions
- When rules conflict, the rule with the higher number wins.
- A request that no rule covers is escalated to a human reviewer.

Rules
Rule 1. When the refund amount is 500 EUR or more: Deny the request.
Rule 2. When the time since purchase is 21 days or higher and the case has the item returned flag set to no: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 3. When the time since purchase is under 21 days and the refund amount is below 200 EUR: Approve the request.
Rule 4. When the fraud alert flag is yes and the time since purchase is above 45 days: Deny the request.
Rule 5. When the time since purchase lies in the range 21 to 30 days inclusive and the bank dispute flag is yes: Deny the request.

Rule 9. When the item returned flag is yes: Approve the request.
Rule 10. When the record shows no for the proof of purchase flag and the record shows yes for the fraud alert flag and the refund amount is at least 300 EUR: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.
Rule 11. When the proof of purchase flag is set to no and the case has the item returned flag set to no: Deny the request.
Rule 12. When the region on record is Dovtor and the time since purchase is more than 60 days: Escalate the request to a human reviewer.

Exceptions
- Rule 12 does not apply when the refund amount is below 500 EUR.
- Rule 10 does not apply when the account age is above 270 days.

q.instructions: Which entry of ledger A does not reconcile with ledger B?

state:
Reconciliation for August 2025. Ledger A is the cash book kept by Ulsture Instruments; ledger B is the bank statement that Welkont Savings Bank sent to Ulsture Instruments.

Matching conventions:
1. An entry of A and a line of B belong together when their reference values are identical, character for character.
2. B is kept by the other side, so every amount figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
3. An entry reconciles when the amount figure on its B line is its own amount figure with the sign reversed and the date rule holds. Split entries, entries with channel CARD and entries with a lodgement number follow their own rules below.
4. The date of a B line may be up to 3 days earlier or later than the date of its A entry; a gap of more than 3 days means the entry does not reconcile.
5. An entry of A may appear in B as two lines with its reference; it then reconciles when the two amount figures add up to its amount with the sign reversed and both lines pass the date rule.
6. Entries of A with channel CARD reach B less a processing fee of 0.30 each: the amount figure on the B line is 0.30 smaller in size than the amount figure in A (the size of a figure is its value without the sign), and its sign is reversed. This holds for plus and minus figures alike. No other channel has a deduction.
7. Several A entries with the same lodgement number are shown in B as a single line carrying that number in the reference column, for the total of those entries with the opposite sign (date rule as usual, against their common date).
8. A combined line that is short by the exact amount of one of its entries means that this one entry is missing from it and does not reconcile, while the rest of the lodgement is fine.
9. B lists its lines in its own order, not in the order of A.
10. A line of B that carries no reference and no lodgement number of A is left aside; it affects no entry.

At most one entry of A fails to reconcile.

q.instructions: Which entry of ledger A does not reconcile with ledger B?

state:
Reconciliation for August 2025. Ledger A is the dispatch register kept at the Mernansa plant; ledger B is the weighbridge record of the haulier Luskivo Haulage.

Conventions for this reconciliation:
1. Each entry of A is matched only with the lines of B that carry exactly the same note id.
2. Lines in B are not sorted the way A is; their position tells nothing.
3. B may hold extra lines whose note id matches nothing in A (no entry, no load number); they play no part.
4. All weight figures in B carry the sign opposite to the one in A.
5. An entry of A is in order when its B line shows the same size of weight figure with the opposite sign, inside the date tolerance. Exceptions follow below for split entries, for packing PALLET and for entries with a load number.
6. The date of a B line may be up to 3 days earlier or later than the date of its A entry; a gap of more than 3 days means the entry does not reconcile.
7. B sometimes splits one entry into two lines with the same note id; together they must give the entry's weight with the opposite sign, and each line must be inside the date tolerance.
8. A line for an entry with packing PALLET is 12.5 kg smaller in size in B (pallet tare; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 12.5 kg in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 12.5 kg. Other packing values carry no deduction.
9. Entries of A that share a load number appear in B as one line whose note id is that number and whose weight figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.
10. If such a combined line falls short of that total, in size, by exactly the weight of one entry of the load, that entry was left out and does not reconcile; the other entries of the load reconcile.

Either exactly one entry of A does not reconcile, or every entry does.

How the two ledgers are matched:
1. Pairing goes by reference alone: an entry of A goes with the B line or lines showing the very same reference.

A line for an entry with channel CARD is 0.20 smaller in size in B (processing fee; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 0.20 in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 0.20. Other channel values carry no deduction.
7. Entries of A that share a lodgement number appear in B as one line whose reference is that number and whose amount figure is their total with the sign reversed; the date rule compares that line with the date the entries share.
8. A combined line that is short by the exact amount of one of its entries means that this one entry is missing from it and does not reconcile, while the rest of the lodgement is fine.
9. B lists its lines in its own order, not in the order of A.

- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between jobs that all rules before it leave level.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each job; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- A job that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- No job can go higher than class 1; a job of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- Once moved, a job competes inside its new class on equal terms with the jobs already there.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "checkin" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- The limit itself counts: 35 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- Both class changes can apply to the same job; it then moves up two classes in total, stopping at class 1.
- A pickup time is due when its time is the current time or earlier; a later one is not due yet.
- The jobs with a due pickup time are level with each other under this rule (the times under "pickup" are not compared), and so are the jobs without a due one.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two jobs have the same one.

Wanted: the job standing third in the order worked out at the current time

Other mode values carry no deduction.
Rule 7: B combines the A entries of one roll-up number into one line with that number as sheet id and their summed hours, sign reversed; their own sheet id values do not appear in B, and the line must be within the date tolerance of their common date.
Rule 8: If such a combined line falls short of that total, in size, by exactly the hours of one entry of the roll-up, that entry was left out and does not reconcile; the other entries of the roll-up reconcile.
Rule 9: Lines in B are not sorted the way A is; their position tells nothing.
Rule 10: Lines of B whose sheet id is neither a sheet id of A nor a roll-up number of A relate to other business and are ignored.

state:
Reconciliation for March 2026. Ledger A is the dispatch register of the Ulsture plant; ledger B is the weighbridge record kept by the haulier Dulvela Haulage.

How the two ledgers are matched:
1. Pairing goes by note id alone: an entry of A goes with the B line or lines showing the very same note id.
2. B lists its lines in its own order, not in the order of A.
3. A line of B that carries no note id and no load number of A is left aside; it affects no entry.
4. B is kept by the other side, so every weight figure appears there with the opposite sign: a plus in A is a minus in B and the other way round.
5. A pair agrees when the B weight figure equals the A weight figure multiplied by -1 and the dates are within the tolerance. The rules below cover the exceptions: split entries, packing PALLET entries and load entries.
6. The date of a B line may be up to 3 days earlier or later than the date of its A entry; a gap of more than 3 days means the entry does not reconcile.
7. Two B lines with the same note id stand for one entry of A; the entry reconciles when their sum equals its weight multiplied by -1 and neither line breaks the date rule.
8. A line for an entry with packing PALLET is 18.5 kg smaller in size in B (pallet tare; size means the figure without its sign) than in A and carries the opposite sign: a plus of size S in A shows as a minus of size S less 18.5 kg in B, and a minus of size S in A as a plus of size S less 18.5 kg. Other packing values carry no deduction.
9. Several A entries with the same load number are shown in B as a single line carrying that number in the note id column, for the total of those entries with the opposite sign (date rule as usual, against their common date).
10. When a combined line is smaller in size than the total by precisely the weight of one of its entries, only that entry fails to reconcile.

Either exactly one entry of A does not reconcile, or every entry does.

The order is fixed by these rules, taken in the order given:
1. Once the waiting time of a task is at least 40 minutes, it is moved up one class.
2. A task with a lower class number goes before a task with a higher class number.
3. Of two tasks, the one with fewer minutes under "runtime" is ahead.
4. Lower ticket number first.

Notes on the rules:
- Read the rules from top to bottom; a later rule is used only to separate tasks that every earlier rule leaves level.
- Rule 1 does not order anything by itself: it sets the class that the later rules use.
- A task that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- There is no class above class 1, so a change that would lead above class 1 stops at class 1.
- Once moved, a task competes inside its new class on equal terms with the tasks already there.
- The waiting time of a task is counted in minutes from the time under "submitted" to the current time; all times are today, on a 24-hour clock.
- The limit itself counts: 40 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- Rank every waiting task once, as things stand at the current time; the position asked for is a place in that ranking.
- Columns and flags that no rule mentions have no effect on the order.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two tasks have the same one.

Rules, applied in the order given:
1. A job that has waited at least 35 minutes moves up one class.
2. Any job carrying the flag "courier" is lifted by one class.
3. The jobs are taken class by class, smallest class number first.
4. Inside a class, every job whose pickup time is due precedes every job whose pickup time is not due.
5. Earlier check-in first.
6. Last tie-break: the job with the lower ticket number goes first.

How to read the rules:
- The rules are applied in the order given: a rule decides only between jobs that all rules before it leave level.
- First apply rules 1 and 2 to each job; from rule 3 on, the word "class" stands for the changed class.
- A job that moves up one class gets the next smaller class number, for instance 3 instead of 4.
- No job can go higher than class 1; a job of class 1 stays in class 1 whatever applies to it.
- Once moved, a job competes inside its new class on equal terms with the jobs already there.
- To get the waiting time, subtract the "checkin" time from the current time (in minutes; same day; 24-hour clock).
- The limit itself counts: 35 minutes of waiting are enough, one minute less is not.
- Both class changes can apply to the same job; it then moves up two classes in total, stopping at class 1.
- A pickup time is due when its time is the current time or earlier; a later one is not due yet.
- The jobs with a due pickup time are level with each other under this rule (the times under "pickup" are not compared), and so are the jobs without a due one.
- All positions (first, second, third) refer to a single order computed at the current time; the clock is not moved in between.
- Only what the rules name counts; any other column or flag changes nothing.
- The ticket number is the number after the dash; no two jobs have the same one.
